clinicalPearls: Monogenic, typically autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene, which disrupt central immune tolerance.
Classic diagnostic triad: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and primary adrenal insufficiency; the diagnosis is usually accepted on two of the three components.
Components tend to accrue in a characteristic sequence, with candidiasis appearing first in infancy or early childhood, followed by hypoparathyroidism and then adrenal insufficiency.
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis reflects neutralising autoantibodies against the cytokines interleukin-17 and interleukin-22.
Neutralising autoantibodies to type I interferons (interferon-omega and interferon-alpha) are a highly sensitive and specific diagnostic marker present in almost all patients.

A wide range of additional features occurs: hypogonadism, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune hepatitis, pernicious anaemia, autoimmune enteropathy, hypothyroidism, alopecia, vitiligo and keratoconjunctivitis.
Ectodermal features include dental enamel hypoplasia and nail dystrophy.
Lifelong surveillance is essential because new components can emerge at any age.
reference.pathophysiology: The AIRE gene is expressed predominantly in medullary thymic epithelial cells, where it drives promiscuous expression of a broad array of tissue-restricted self-antigens. This presentation mediates negative selection of autoreactive developing thymocytes and supports generation of regulatory T cells. Loss-of-function AIRE mutations impair this central tolerance, allowing autoreactive T and B lymphocytes to escape to the periphery and mount organ-specific autoimmune destruction across multiple endocrine and non-endocrine tissues. High-titre neutralising autoantibodies against type I interferons are a near-universal serological hallmark, while neutralising autoantibodies against interleukin-17 and interleukin-22 impair mucosal antifungal defence and produce the characteristic chronic candidiasis. The result is a progressive, cumulative multisystem autoimmune disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (Schmidt syndrome), which is polygenic and typically adult-onset
Isolated autoimmune Addison disease or isolated autoimmune hypoparathyroidism
IPEX syndrome (FOXP3 mutation) with enteropathy and endocrinopathy
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis from STAT1 gain-of-function or other inborn errors of immunity
Common variable immunodeficiency with autoimmune manifestations
additionalInvestigations: Autoantibodies against interferon-omega/interferon-alpha as a highly sensitive screening marker
Adrenal (21-hydroxylase) autoantibodies with morning cortisol, adrenocorticotrophin stimulation and plasma adrenocorticotrophin
Calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone to detect hypoparathyroidism
Organ-specific autoantibody panel (islet/GAD, thyroid, parietal cell and intrinsic factor, tissue transglutaminase, liver)
Fungal swabs and cultures to confirm candidiasis, liver function tests and a full blood count for pernicious anaemia
Assessment for functional hyposplenism and ongoing monitoring for autoimmune hepatitis
redFlags: Adrenal crisis, which may be precipitated when thyroxine is started before glucocorticoid replacement
Hypocalcaemic tetany, laryngospasm or seizures from hypoparathyroidism
Oral squamous cell carcinoma arising within areas of chronic candidiasis
Life-threatening infection related to functional asplenia
reference.prognosis: A chronic lifelong disorder with substantial morbidity; with vigilant hormone replacement and monitoring most patients do well, but mortality relates to adrenal crisis, severe hypocalcaemia, fulminant hepatitis, sepsis and oral carcinoma.
pitfalls: Starting levothyroxine before excluding or treating adrenal insufficiency, which can precipitate an adrenal crisis.
Diagnosing a single component in isolation and failing to anticipate the syndrome and its future manifestations.
Attributing recurrent candidiasis to a simple immunodeficiency without considering APS-1.
Missing evolving components because they may appear many years apart.
Neglecting surveillance for oral carcinoma in longstanding mucocutaneous candidiasis.
